title: As he sat on his lowbacked car, both black, one full, one lean, walk towards the railway bridge, to be married by Father Maher
html_source: A version of The Low-backed Car by Samuel Lover contains the lines “I’d rather own that car, sir, / With Peggy by my side / Than a coach and four and gold galore / And a lady for my bride.” The concluding lyrics: “As we drove in the low-back’d car, / To be married by Father Maher.” Stephen’s “mis-translation about the ships being bridged may not be incidental to Joyce’s intentions here if the scene is to portray a commercial partnership, or "marriage”, one, as with the familiar form of marriage, merely combines a commercial arrangement and an emotional commitment (without the physical involvement in this case). Perhaps Bloom’s preference at this end of this day which saw a betrayal of his actual marriage, would be for the monetary benefits of joining with Stephen/Peggy over having a “lady as for [his] bride.
